title: Beyond the U.S.-China Binary: The New Landscape of AI Partnerships in the Global South
gist: Sabeen Dhanani maps a multipolar AI-partnership landscape in the Global South: China spans the full stack and is moving into governance, India offers open/local AI, the Gulf sells compute, middle powers work via multilaterals, while the US relies on commercial exports and is losing developer mindshare to Chinese open-weight models.

insights.claim: Chinese models accounted for 41 percent of Hugging Face downloads by early 2026, surpassing US-developed models, and African developers in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria build on Alibaba's Qwen, DeepSeek and Moonshot AI largely on cost.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Chinese open-weight models are winning developer adoption in emerging markets, pressuring US model vendors' reach.
insights.locator: China Moves Beyond Infrastructure to Governance

insights.claim: China launched the Shanghai-headquartered World AI Cooperation Organization with 29 founding members, and Xi pledged 5,000 AI training slots for the Global South over five years in July 2026, shifting from infrastructure to influence over AI rules.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: China is competing to set global AI governance norms alongside selling infrastructure.
insights.locator: China Moves Beyond Infrastructure to Governance

insights.claim: India promotes open, multilingual, affordable AI through the IndiaAI Mission, BharatGen, AI4Bharat and Sarvam AI, building on digital public infrastructure like Aadhaar and UPI.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: India is a credible alternative supplier of open AI stacks to developing markets.
insights.locator: India Prioritizes Open-Source and Locally Relevant AI

insights.claim: Gulf data center capacity is projected to grow from roughly 1 gigawatt in 2025 to more than 3.3 gigawatts by 2030, and Saudi PIF aims to be 'the prime backend provider of compute-as-a-service for emerging markets across Africa and Asia'.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Gulf compute-export ambitions are a data center and chip demand driver.
insights.quote: the prime backend provider of compute-as-a-service for emerging markets across Africa and Asia

insights.claim: The $1 billion Kenya data center project announced by G42 and Microsoft in 2024 stalled in 2026 because Kenya's grid could not support it and payment terms were not agreed, showing exporting Gulf compute to lower-income markets is harder than advertised.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Power-grid and payment constraints cap emerging-market data center rollouts.

insights.claim: Middle powers including South Korea, Italy, Spain and Singapore extend influence through UN, World Bank and regional bodies, and Finland and Norway led a September 2026 'Call for Control of Frontier AI Models' backed by Canada, Kenya, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Turkey and the UAE.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A coalition outside the US and China is pushing frontier AI safety standards.
insights.locator: Middle Powers Work Through Multilateral and Regional Institutions

insights.claim: The US is largely absent as a development actor in Global South AI even as US hyperscalers invest, with Microsoft committing $1.7 billion in Indonesia and $2.2 billion in Malaysia and Amazon Web Services over $5 billion in Mexico over 15 years.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: US firms win commercially, but government efforts focus on exports without building local capacity.

insights.claim: The multipolar landscape gives developing countries leverage in choosing partners, as Kenya works with Chinese firms, US hyperscalers, Gulf investors, India and multilaterals, but will fragment AI standards and governance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Expect no single stack winner and fragmented standards, which complicates compliance for global AI vendors.
